Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.

text:
**Why Primary Schools Should Keep Teaching Joined Handwriting**

Every few years a headline announces that handwriting is finished. Children type on tablets from the age of three, the argument goes, so why should a seven year old spend precious classroom hours learning to loop an l and tail a y? Some countries have already dropped joined writing from their curriculums, and many teachers privately wonder whether they should follow. I think they should not. Primary schools ought to keep teaching joined handwriting, not out of nostalgia but because it still does real work for children. It builds fluency, supports spelling and thinking, helps children with certain learning differences, and gives every pupil a practical skill they will use for the rest of their lives. The case for abandoning it rests on a picture of the future that is less certain than its supporters admit.

Start with the most practical point, which is speed and ease. Printing letters one at a time forces the writer to lift the pen after every stroke. Each lift is a small interruption, and across a page of text those interruptions add up. Joined writing lets the hand travel in a flowing motion, and once a child has mastered it the pen moves faster with less effort. Anyone who has watched a confident writer take notes in a lecture knows the difference. The joined hand keeps pace with the speaker while the printed hand falls behind and starts to cramp. Primary school is where the foundations of that fluency are laid. If we skip it, we ask children to reach secondary school and exams with a writing style that tires them out, and then we wonder why so many struggle to finish a timed paper.

This matters because handwriting is not going away from the places where children are judged. Written examinations remain the main way that pupils around the world show what they know. A teenager sitting a three hour history paper must produce several pages of legible text under pressure. Examiners cannot award marks for words they cannot read. Children who never learned an efficient joined hand are more likely to write slowly, to write illegibly when they hurry, or to write too little. The promise that everything will soon be typed has been made for thirty years, and yet the exam hall still smells of pencil shavings and nervous sweat. A school that ignores this reality is gambling with its pupils' results.

The second argument concerns the mind rather than the hand. A growing body of research suggests that writing by hand engages the brain differently from typing. Studies using brain imaging have found that children who write letters by hand show more activity in regions linked to reading and language than children who only type or trace on a screen. Other research has found that students who take notes by hand often understand and remember lectures better than those who type, partly because the slower pace forces them to summarise rather than transcribe. Joined writing sits within this picture. Because the letters are connected, the child must think about the shape of the whole word, about how one letter leads into the next. This is a kind of motor memory for spelling. Many teachers report that children who write words in a single flowing movement remember the patterns of those words more securely than children who build them from separate pieces.

It would be dishonest to claim that the evidence is settled, and I will not pretend otherwise. Some researchers argue that the benefits come from handwriting in general and that there is little proof that joined letters beat careful print. That is a fair challenge. But notice what it does and does not show. It shows that handwriting matters, which is the very thing the abolitionists deny. And the absence of a decisive trial is not a reason to throw away a practice that has served children for centuries. When we cannot be sure which style is best, the sensible course is to keep teaching the one that has the practical advantage of speed and the plausible advantage of better spelling memory, rather than to dismantle it on a hunch.

Third, consider the children who find school hardest. Many specialists who work with dyslexia and related difficulties have long recommended joined writing. The reasoning is simple and quite persuasive. A child who prints often reverses letters such as b and d, because the two forms look like mirror images and each begins with a separate stroke. In a joined script the letters start from a common entry point and carry a built in direction, which makes reversals less likely. The continuous flow also gives the child a rhythm to follow, and that rhythm can reduce the confusion about where one letter ends and the next begins. For a child with weaker fine motor control, a well taught joined hand can also be less tiring than the stop and start effort of print. If we remove joined writing from the curriculum, we remove a tool that some of our most vulnerable learners rely on.

There is also a point about fairness that rarely gets a hearing. Children from homes with plenty of books, devices and quiet time to practise will learn to write well whatever the school does. Children from poorer homes often depend on the classroom for almost everything. If schools stop teaching a skilled and fluent hand, families who can afford tutors and handwriting workbooks will keep supplying it, and families who cannot will not. Over time a neat, confident hand becomes a quiet marker of privilege. Teaching it to everyone, deliberately and well, is one small way of keeping that door open. Public education has always been about giving all children the same starting kit, and handwriting is part of the kit.

The strongest objection to my view is the argument from time. The school day is crowded. Teachers must cover reading, mathematics, science, music, physical education, and now computing and online safety. Every ten minutes spent on looping letters is ten minutes taken from something else, and children who will type most of their adult lives surely need keyboard skills more than pen skills. I take this seriously, but I think it misjudges both the cost and the benefit. The cost is small. A few short and focused sessions each week, in the middle years of primary school, are enough to teach most children a fluent joined hand. And the benefits do not compete with digital skills. They complement them. A child can learn to touch type and to write by hand, just as a child can learn to swim and to ride a bicycle. Treating the two as rivals is a false choice. Most adults use both every single day, scribbling a shopping list in the morning and answering emails at noon.

Another objection says that handwriting is only a means to an end, and that if a machine can produce the words faster, the means no longer matters. This misunderstands what school is for. We teach children to write by hand for the same reason we teach them to add by hand before handing them a calculator. The manual skill builds understanding that the shortcut skips. A child who has felt how a word is formed, who has struggled with the shape of a capital G and finally mastered it, has a deeper relationship with written language than a child who only pressed a key. Moreover, handwriting carries something that typing cannot. A handwritten letter, a birthday card, a signature on a form, a note left on a kitchen table, all of these carry a trace of the person. Children who cannot write a fluent hand lose access to that quiet form of expression, and to the ability to read the handwritten words of their grandparents.

That last point deserves more weight than it usually gets. If joined writing disappears from schools, then within a generation large numbers of people will be unable to read it. Archives full of letters, diaries, wills, recipes and wartime notes are written in cursive. Family papers that were once treasured will become unreadable to the very people they were meant for. Some American students already report that they cannot make out the handwriting on a historical document or even on a teacher's comments. A society that cannot read its own handwritten past has made itself a little poorer. Teaching children to write in a joined hand is the surest way to teach them to read one.

None of this means schools should cling to old methods without thought. The way joined writing is taught can and should improve. Too many children are drilled in elaborate scripts with decorative loops that no adult actually uses. The best approach is a simple, practical joined hand, taught early enough to prevent bad habits, with joins that are easy to form and that real writers will keep using. Schools should also be sensible about expectations. Not every child will develop beautiful penmanship, and that is fine. The goal is legible, comfortable, reasonably quick writing, not calligraphy. Teachers should be given proper training in how to teach it, because handwriting is too often handed to whoever has a spare moment and left to chance.

In the end, the question is not whether children should learn to type. Of course they should. The question is whether a skill that is quick, that probably helps memory and spelling, that assists children with learning difficulties, that remains essential in examinations, and that connects us to our written past is worth a modest place in the primary timetable. I believe it plainly is. The costs are low and the benefits are broad. Those who would abandon it ask us to bet that handwriting will vanish, and they offer little evidence that it will. Those who would keep it ask only that we continue to give children a tool that has worked well for a very long time. When the risks fall on seven year olds, caution is the wiser course. Keep the loop, and keep the link.
